questions.title: How can a plaintiff have standing to seek penalties that are paid to the government rather than to themselves?
questions.question_body: I'm struggling with the MFLSA portion of the opinion. The court notes that the statutory penalties are payable to the Commissioner, not to the plaintiff (Cohen). Usually, standing requires a 'concrete and particularized' injury. If the plaintiff isn't receiving the money, how does seeking a government penalty satisfy the requirements for standing? The court mentions 'redress' in terms of deterring future violations, but I'm confused about how that works in a private civil suit.

questions.title: Does a 'voluntary cessation' of a challenged practice automatically moot a claim for statutory penalties?
questions.question_body: In the MFLSA analysis, the court discusses whether the claim is moot if Consilio's overtime policy is no longer in place. They mention that 'voluntary cessation' doesn't normally deprive a court of power, but then say the claim 'might' become moot if it's clear the conduct won't recur. I don't understand the distinction here—if the employer just changes the policy to make the case go away, does the employee lose their right to seek penalties for the past violation?

questions.title: Why does the 'Legislature knows how' argument prevent a plaintiff from recovering penalties under the MPWA?
questions.question_body: The court ruled that Cohen couldn't get average daily wage penalties under § 181.101 because only the Commissioner is mentioned. They then pointed to other sections of the law (like § 181.13) where the legislature explicitly allowed employees to collect penalties. Is this a standard rule of statutory interpretation? Essentially, if the legislature gave the right in one section but didn't explicitly give it in another, does that automatically mean the right is excluded from the second section, even if 'appropriate relief' is mentioned?

questions.title: Can a party request a different form of injunctive relief in a summary judgment brief without amending their complaint?
questions.question_body: Cohen originally sought specific injunctive relief in his complaint but later asked the court to order the rescission of the 2019 policy in his summary judgment briefing. The court dismissed this, stating that new claims must be raised through amended complaints under Rule 15. I'm confused because I thought the 'relief' requested could be flexible as long as the underlying legal claim was already pleaded. Why does changing the specific remedy require a formal amendment to the complaint?

questions.title: What constitutes a 'waiver' of an issue on appeal when the lower court failed to address the claim?
questions.question_body: Regarding the MWTA claim, the district court apparently provided 'little to no discussion' of the issue. However, the Eighth Circuit refused to disturb the order because Cohen's appeal brief lacked sufficient legal authority. If the district court failed to properly analyze the claim in the first place, is the appellate court's refusal to review it based on the quality of the brief a standard application of the waiver doctrine, or is the plaintiff expected to 'save' the issue through an exceptionally strong brief?
